overview: Gugustus's Disabler is a collection of independent packet-bypass modes gated by individual BooleanValue toggles and dispatched from a single outgoing-packet event. The blanket switches cancel keepalives, status pings, entity actions, abilities and inventory transactions outright; the ping-spoof mode parks keepalive echoes and releases them late from a render-3D tick so the server measures inflated latency; and the anticheat-specific modes run movement exploits for HAC, AAC5 and NCP, a transaction-uid flip for UniversoCraft, a self-spectate injector, a Badlion brand rewrite, and a receive-side S08 teleport eater that re-sends the teleport target as a movement packet.

sections.p: All interception funnels through one method: onEventSendPacket branches on instanceof over the outgoing packet, and each branch is gated by its own BooleanValue. onEventUpdate runs once per tick and carries the movement exploits (HAC, AAC5, NCPTimerSemi, RoyalPixels), onEventRender3D acts as the flush clock for parked keepalives, and onRecv handles the incoming S08 teleport eater. Module state is an ArrayList of CustomC00PacketKeepAlive entries and a boolean 'disabling' flag that the UniversoCraft mode arms and clears. A world-change handler turns the module off when DisableOnWorld is set, so cancellation modes cannot survive a respawn or a server switch.

The ping spoof is a buffer-and-flush cycle with no timer thread. Every 40 network ticks the server stamps a fresh key, sends it in S00PacketKeepAlive, and stores it; the vanilla client replies with C00 carrying that exact key, and processKeepAlive folds the round trip into the ping as (ping * 3 + elapsed) / 4, but only when the echoed key matches the stored one. The module intercepts that echo, parks it with a release time of now plus the delay setting plus 0-200ms of jitter, and cancels it; onEventRender3D re-sends expired entries through addToSendQueueDirect, which bypasses the event bus so a flush is never re-buffered. The echo keeps its original key, so the server accepts it whenever it lands and the measured latency becomes the delay. The NoFlag receive handler is the inverse trick: it cancels an S08 teleport closer than 8 blocks and re-sends the teleport's absolute target as a C06, so the server-side position converges while the client never snaps.

The movement modes lean on gaps in vanilla processPlayer validation. The illegal-position check bounds only x and z at 3.0E7 and never touches y, so the AAC5 mode's first C06 (y minus 1.0E159, z plus 10, onGround true) cannot be kicked; the second C06 re-asserts the real position, converging the server entity before the outlier matters. The moved-too-quickly check squares min(delta, motion) per axis, so with server-side motion near zero a large delta like the HAC mode's 11-block drop (every 10 ticks, onGround true) stays under the 100 threshold. NCPTimerSemi shifts the local position down 0.017 per tick and sets motionY to 0.019, a two-line desync with no packet of its own. RoyalPixels streams C13 packets claiming allowFlying and flying, which the server only applies when its own capabilities allow flying. The UniversoCraft branch arms a 'disabling' flag from movement in the first 10 ticks, clears it on a C02 attack, and while it is set under tick 350 rewrites every C0F uid to Short.MIN_VALUE or Short.MAX_VALUE on alternating ticks; processConfirmTransaction only re-enables crafting when the echoed uid equals the recorded short, so those confirmations never validate.

files.label: Disabler.java
files.explanation:
onEventSendPacket is the single interception point for every packet the client is about to send, and each branch is a separate toggle. The blanket switches are the simplest: keepAlive cancels every C00 echo, entityAction cancels all C0B packets, playerAbilities cancels C13 packets, and confirmTransaction cancels every C0F. Each one removes a class of traffic the server expects, so each is only usable against servers that tolerate the gap. The ping switch is different: C01PacketPing is a status-phase packet, so in play that branch never fires; it is a leftover from clients that spoof the in-game ping through the status handler.

The ping spoof is built around the vanilla keepalive exchange. The server issues S00PacketKeepAlive roughly every two seconds, recording the key it sent; the vanilla client echoes C00PacketKeepAlive with the identical key, and the server's processKeepAlive accepts any echo whose key matches and folds the elapsed time into the player's ping average. The module intercepts the outgoing echo, builds a CustomC00PacketKeepAlive whose release time is now plus the delay setting plus 0-200ms of random jitter, and cancels the original. onEventRender3D then walks the buffer and, whenever a release time has passed, pushes a fresh C00PacketKeepAlive with the same key through addToSendQueueDirect. Because that path bypasses the event bus, the flushed echo is not re-intercepted, and because the key is preserved, the server accepts the late echo and records the inflated round trip as ping. The delay is capped at 4000ms on purpose: an echo whose key has already been superseded by the next keepalive is silently dropped by the key comparison.

The tick handler runs the movement exploits, and all of them survive vanilla because of two facts about processPlayer. The illegal-position check bounds only x and z at 3.0E7, never y, so the AAC5 mode's first C06 (y minus 1.0E159, z plus 10, yaw and pitch 0, onGround true) is not kicked; the immediately following C06 re-asserting the real position converges the server entity before the outlier matters. The moved-too-quickly check squares min(delta, motion) per axis, so with server-side motion near zero a large delta like the HAC mode's 11-block drop (sent every 10 ticks, onGround true) stays under the 100 threshold. NCPTimerSemi takes a different route: it nudges the local position down 0.017 each tick and sets motionY to 0.019, a two-line desync with no packet of its own. RoyalPixels streams C13 packets with allowFlying and flying set, a claim the server-side handler only applies when the server's own capabilities already grant flying.

The UniversoCraft branch runs a state machine over the outgoing stream. Movement packets inside the first 10 ticks arm the 'disabling' flag, a C02 use-entity attack clears it, and while the flag is set and ticksExisted is below 350 every C0F has its uid rewritten to Short.MIN_VALUE on even ticks or Short.MAX_VALUE on odd ticks. The check against S07PacketRespawn that also arms the flag is unreachable inside an outgoing-packet handler, so it is dead code. Vanilla's processConfirmTransaction re-enables container crafting only when the echoed uid equals the short it recorded for that window, so the flipped confirmations never validate and the transaction tracking the UniversoCraft setup relies on stays broken.

onRecv holds the NoFlag teleport eater: an S08 arriving after tick 20 whose target lies within 8 blocks (Euclidean distance) is cancelled and re-sent as a C06 with the target's x, y, z, yaw and pitch, so the server-side correction lands without the client-side snap that vanilla's handlePlayerPosLook would apply. The 8-block cutoff and the tick-20 guard leave real teleports (spawn, portals) untouched, and the debug toggle prints a chat line when the eater fires. The spectate mode injects C18PacketSpectate with the player's own UUID alongside every C03; vanilla only honors spectate requests in spectator mode, so on survival servers the packet exists purely to disturb anticheats that watch the traffic. The BLC spoof replaces the payload of C17 on the MC|Brand channel, the packet the vanilla client sends once at join carrying ClientBrandRetriever.getClientModName(); the fresh buffer writes the string "blc" so brand fingerprinting classifies the client as Badlion.

files.label: CustomC00PacketKeepAlive.java (ping-spoof carrier)
files.explanation:
The carrier subclasses the vanilla C00PacketKeepAlive and adds exactly one thing: a final long time that holds the absolute release deadline. The constructor forwards the keepalive key to the superclass, so the inherited key field and its VarInt serialization are untouched; the added field never reaches the wire, which is what makes the class safe to park in a list and re-emit later as a plain C00PacketKeepAlive(key). The key is what the server's processKeepAlive compares against the value it stored when it sent the matching S00, so preserving it unchanged is the entire point of the subclass.

The Disabler creates one of these per intercepted echo, computing the deadline as System.currentTimeMillis() plus the delay setting plus 0-200ms of jitter, and stores it in the keepAlivePackets list instead of letting the original packet through. The render-3D flush loop then compares packet.getTime() against System.currentTimeMillis() and turns expired entries back into fresh C00PacketKeepAlive objects via getKey(), which is why the class only needs the key and a timestamp. The carrier never appears in the module's own event stream, so a buffered echo cannot loop back into the interception branch. The same carrier class ships in the Augustus b2.6 and Xenza B9 branches of the client lineage.

countering.label: KeepAliveFrequency (keepalive ledger)
countering.explanation:
NoCheatPlus replaces vanilla's accept-any-echo keepalive model with an id-tracked ledger. The ProtocolLib KeepAliveAdapter records every outgoing S00 id into NetData.keepAliveRequests (pruned after KEEP_ALIVE_REQUEST_MAX_AGE_MS = 30000ms, capped at 40 pending), and recordKeepAlivePacket matches each incoming C00 against that list: a reply with a matching pending request sets keepAliveExpectedResponse, while a reply with no pending request or with a duplicate id is counted. Every incoming C00 is timestamped into keepAliveFreq, an ActionFrequency(20, 1000) (NetData line 150), so one-second buckets over a 20-second window; the check bails while a response is still expected unless the id is a duplicate, then flags when the newest bucket scores above 1f (more than one reply in the same second), with the duplicate-id path tightening the first-bucket limit to 1f. The full-window score also flags more than one unexpected reply per second sustained over the window.

The ping-spoof mode parks each intercepted echo as a CustomC00PacketKeepAlive with a release time of now plus delay plus 0-200ms jitter and flushes every expired entry from one onEventRender3D tick through addToSendQueueDirect, so the check's ledger is exactly what the spoof's failure modes run into. A render-loop stall (lag spike, minimized window, loading screen) makes several parked echoes expire together and the flush lands them all in the same second, and any echo whose request aged out of the 30-second window, was dropped by the 40-entry pending cap, or was cleared by a world change or rejoin arrives as an unexpected reply that feeds the frequency counter; two or more such replies in one bucket trip the violation. The duplicate path matters because the module preserves the original key when re-sending, so a replayed id is never forgiven. The blanket keepAlive cancel is the one mode this check cannot see: no reply ever arrives, nothing is counted, and the expected-response guard keeps the check dormant until the request is pruned, so outright cancellation is left to the server-side keepalive timeout.

Tolerance and bypass surface: the check allows one reply per second (a vanilla client echoes one S00 per ~2s interval), forgives small monotonic id runs only when outgoing tracking was never seen, and has a startup grace period. A client that delays a single echo inside the request window and never replays an id passes by design: the module's 4000ms delay cap sits far inside the 30s request age, so each delayed echo still matches its pending request and the bail applies. The check defeats the burst, duplicate and unexpected-echo forms of keepalive spoofing, which is the class of behavior the module produces whenever its flush backs up; the steady-state one-echo-per-request delay is its known tolerance.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement physics envelope)
countering.explanation:
SurvivalFly rebuilds the client's physics envelope from the world instead of trusting the packet. In check() (line 114) the horizontal allowance comes from prepareSpeedEstimation and the vertical allowance from vDistRel (line 1839, invoked at line 212), and the violation is (max(hDistanceAboveLimit, 0.0) + max(yDistanceAboveLimit, 0.0)) * 100 (line 233), with handleViolation set-backs the player to the stored setBack location. vDistRel initializes the allowed vertical distance from the previous move's momentum (lastMove.yDistance, line 1932) and only accepts a few named envelopes: a zero-y move on ground (line 1882), a jump (line 1889), a step-up (line 1899) and a riptide launch. Critically, fromOnGround and toOnGround come from RichBoundsLocation.isOnGround(), which scans the actual block cache at minY minus yOnGround, not from the packet's onGround flag, so claiming onGround does not relax the envelope.

That removes the vanilla gaps the movement modes lean on. The HAC mode's 11-block drop (one C06 with y minus 11 and onGround true every 10 ticks) presents a yDistance of -11 against an allowed descent of a few tenths of a block per tick, so yDistanceAboveLimit is around 10.6 and the result is over 1000, an immediate violation and set-back; the packet's onGround true is ignored because NCP's own ray trace says the claimed spot is air. The AAC5 mode's first C06 with y minus 1.0E159 produces a yDistanceAboveLimit several orders of magnitude beyond the envelope, so the violation fires on that first packet before the second C06 can re-assert the real position, and because the check compares per-move deltas to a physics model, the vanilla illegal-position gap (bounds on x and z only) that the module exploits does not exist here. The NoFlag S08 eater is the one mode this check does not flag: the server still processes the S08 teleport, resets its tracking, and the re-sent C06 re-asserting the teleport target is a zero-distance move from the teleported position.

Tolerance and bypass surface: any per-tick vertical delta inside the gravity, jump or step envelope with continuous momentum passes, and the check is forgiving of genuine fall momentum. The module's drop-based modes exceed the envelope by design, so no tuning keeps the exploit while passing the check; the only Gugustus mode that slips under the vertical envelope is NCPTimerSemi, whose 0.017-block per-tick downward drift sits inside the modeled fall acceleration and is invisible to vDistRel.

countering.label: MorePackets (movement packet rate)
countering.explanation:
MorePackets counts the raw rate of serverbound move packets, content-blind. MovingListener invokes morePackets.check on every processed move (line 1561), each of which is scored into data.morePacketsFreq, an ActionFrequency with 500ms buckets (MovingData line 321) covering the configured window, and NetStatic.morePacketsCheck (NetStatic line 63) accumulates the window score against cc.morePacketsEPSMax, default 22 packets per second with 20 ideal, plus a burst path on the newest half-second bucket (default 15 packets, direct-violation 10, burst events 95 per minute) with lag adaption via TickTask. A violation returns the morePacketsSetBack location, seeded from the SurvivalFly set-back when one exists, so the player is snapped back on top of the movement check.

The AAC5 mode is the direct target: it sends two C06 packets per tick, roughly 40 per second sustained, so the window accumulator runs at nearly double the 22/s ceiling and vEPSAcc stays positive for the whole window (fullCount minus maxPackets times window duration), tagging epsacc and canceling at vl>2 under the default actions. The HAC mode's extra C06 every 10 ticks adds only 0.1/s and is negligible to the accumulator, and the NoFlag S08 eater's re-sent C06 adds one packet per teleport, so those two only matter when teleports concentrate; the half-second burst path is what catches a concentrated flush of extra C06s. The check never inspects y, so the AAC5 outlier position counts the same as any other packet, and because it scores every move including the correcting second C06, the mode cannot shed its doubled rate by fixing its position.

Tolerance and bypass surface: the check burns idle windows at the ideal 20/s rate and redistributes excess into later empty buckets, so short spikes under the window ceiling are forgiven; staying at or under 22/s sustained with fewer than 15 packets in any half second passes. Among the Gugustus modes only AAC5's doubled per-tick packets breach that rate by design; the module's other modes add too few packets for the accumulator to notice, which is why this check pairs with SurvivalFly rather than replacing it.

countering.label: NoFall (faked onGround)
countering.explanation:
Vrekt's NoFall cross-checks the client's claimed onGround flag against a server-computed ground state. The MovingListener derives ground from the world: onGround = LocationHelper.isOnGround(to, vertical) and the location is stored as groundLocation whenever it is grounded, while the PacketListener records the raw packet flag into MovingData via setFlyingClientOnGround(flying.getOnGround()). NoFall.check then fires when the vertical distance from the last grounded location is at least 3.0 blocks, the player is descending, Vrekt's own ground state says the player is not on the ground, and yet the client claimed onGround while the server-side fall distance is zero, raising the violation "Fall distance is 0 while not onGround. (Client faked)" and applying damage(toGround) when it cancels.

This is a direct hit on the HAC mode's payload. The mode's C06 with y minus 11 and onGround true every 10 ticks relies on the packet flag doing two jobs in vanilla: resetting fallDistance to zero and keeping the movedTooQuickly check lenient. Vrekt ignores the flag for ground purposes, so the same packet presents an 11-block descent from the last grounded location while its own ground calculation reports air, and the claimed onGround is exposed as a lie the instant the move is processed. The AAC5 mode's C06s, which also travel with onGround true, hit the same contradiction whenever the claimed position sits 3 or more blocks below the grounded location while descending.

Tolerance and bypass surface: the check needs a 3-block descent threshold, real descending motion, and a zero fall distance to trigger, so small hops and genuine landings pass. The bypass is to send onGround true only when the position actually touches ground, which is exactly the advantage the HAC and AAC5 modes exist to fake: the mode either claims onGround over open air and trips NoFall, or drops the claim and takes fall damage and the SurvivalFly envelope instead. The one Gugustus mode outside this check is the S08 eater, since it never fakes ground, it only cancels a client-side teleport snap.
